rationale: Start with a broad gradient at an intermediate temperature to locate the full elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds.

Only the first pair needs improvement. Raising temperature while keeping the gradient fixed tests temperature-driven selectivity and should shorten retention, preserving room below the 10-minute time threshold.
Injection 2 reached the maximum CRF. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method, checking whether the first pair retains R ≥ 1.5.

Lowering phi1 to 0.85 makes the gradient slightly shallower than injection 3, aiming to restore first-pair resolution above 1.5 while remaining faster than injection 2. The endpoint remains comfortably above the observed last-peak elution composition.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving injection 4's slope to reduce retention and test the first pair's sensitivity to starting composition. Injection 4 remains a fully resolved, maximum-score fallback.

Use a slightly steeper gradient than injection 4 to reduce retention while targeting first-pair resolution just above 1.5. The 0.70 endpoint remains above the last peak's estimated elution composition, so all peaks should elute during the gradient.

This slightly steeper gradient tests the first pair near its full-resolution limit while shortening the programmed gradient. The last compound may elute during the final hold, so its retention will determine whether the lower endpoint offers a net time benefit.

With a maximum-score method secured, test a cooler, steeper gradient for an alternative selectivity regime; peak identities are unknown, so the earlier temperature comparison cannot rule out an order reversal. The broad endpoint should ensure complete elution despite lower temperature.

Keep temperature fixed and steepen the gradient to test whether the late three-peak cluster separates through slope-dependent selectivity. The first pair has some resolution margin, and this run should shorten retention while probing a potentially faster alternative.

The late cluster responded poorly to slope alone, so raise temperature one step relative to injection 8 to test selective separation. This checks whether the cooler-temperature branch can resolve all pairs with a shorter gradient.

Raise temperature another step to separate the late cluster and increase the starting organic fraction to shorten retention. The narrower gradient window also reduces slope, which may help preserve resolution of the early pair.

Use a narrower gradient window to improve the first pair and preserve separation of the late cluster. Raising the starting fraction partly offsets the retention increase from the shallower slope, testing another route to a compact, fully resolved method.

Return to the successful high-temperature regime and test a slope just steeper than injection 7. This probes whether first-pair resolution remains at least 1.5 while a higher endpoint avoids the final hold and potentially reduces last-peak retention.

At the higher starting fraction, reduce the slope relative to injection 5 to recover first-pair resolution. This tests whether a shifted, shallower window can provide full resolution with competitive retention time.

Test a shallower gradient in the 35 °C regime, where the late cluster was already resolved but the first pair remained limiting. Lowering the starting fraction relative to injection 11 should also help retain and separate the early pair.

Test whether a further upward shift in starting composition, paired with a shallower slope, can maintain full resolution of the early pair. This extends the window optimization while keeping a sufficiently strong endpoint for complete elution.

The fastest fully resolved method has little first-pair resolution margin. Test a modestly shallower gradient to increase that margin while keeping all peaks within 10 minutes and preserving the maximum CRF.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 17 to shorten retention while retaining more first-pair resolution margin than the fastest fully resolved method. This should provide another maximum-CRF option between injections 4 and 17.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 14 at the same starting composition and temperature, aiming to shorten retention while keeping the first pair fully resolved. The high endpoint ensures the last peak remains within the gradient.

Test whether 30 °C improves the early pair while a shallower gradient resolves the late cluster seen in injection 10. The elevated starting fraction should offset some of the added retention, with the established 60 °C methods retained as maximum-score fallbacks.

At 35 °C, use a shallower slope than injection 11 to improve the limiting early pair while preserving late-cluster separation. The 0.80 endpoint should avoid the prolonged final hold seen in injection 20 and keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Trim the upper gradient window and shorten the programmed gradient relative to injection 14, with a slightly shallower slope to preserve first-pair resolution. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition, so this should retain maximum CRF without a prolonged final hold.

Test a shallower gradient to increase the first pair's resolution margin while targeting complete elution before 10 minutes. Monitor the third–fourth pair, whose resolution has decreased as the gradient becomes shallower; injection 7 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.

Slightly steepen the slope relative to injection 23 to shorten retention and improve the third–fourth pair, while retaining substantial first-pair resolution. This targets balanced resolution margins at maximum CRF; injection 7 remains the fastest fully resolved option observed.

Finish with a trimmed gradient expected to retain maximum CRF and more first-pair resolution margin than injection 7, with the last peak near 8 minutes. Injection 7 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed; this final run tests a shorter programmed gradient than the higher-margin alternatives.
